title: CFA Level I - Session 1 Mock Exam (Paper 1)
description: Full-length 90-question, professional-grade mock exam featuring complex vignettes, realistic calculations, and deep-dive scenarios replicating the true CFA exam difficulty.

questions.text: An economist observes that in the country of Avalon, the central bank has recently engaged in open market sales of government securities, increased the reserve requirement from 9% to 13%, and raised the policy rate by 25 basis points. Concurrently, the government has reduced infrastructure spending and increased corporate tax rates. The combined effect of these monetary and fiscal policies on Avalon's aggregate demand (AD) is most likely to be:
options: Strongly contractionary.
Strongly expansionary.
Indeterminate without knowing the relative magnitudes.
questions.hint: Analyze whether each policy increases or decreases the money supply and government injections.
questions.explanation: Open market sales, higher reserve requirements, higher policy rates, reduced spending, and higher taxes all act to contract the economy and reduce aggregate demand.

questions.text: Sarah Jenkins, CFA, is a portfolio manager at Vanguard Analytics. She recently received a non-public research report from her firm's equity analyst regarding a potential acquisition of AeroDynamics. The report concludes that AeroDynamics is severely undervalued. Before the report is distributed to clients, Sarah Jenkins purchases 5000 shares of AeroDynamics for her personal account and 19000 shares for her largest institutional client. According to the CFA Institute Standards of Professional Conduct, Sarah Jenkins has most likely violated the standard relating to:
options: Priority of Transactions and Material Nonpublic Information.
Loyalty, Prudence, and Care only.
Fair Dealing and Diligence.
questions.hint: Consider the rules around trading on information before clients and trading on non-public info.
questions.explanation: By trading for her personal account before clients, she violates Priority of Transactions. By acting on a non-public internal report regarding an acquisition, she may also be acting on material nonpublic information depending on the source.

questions.text: Consider a portfolio composed of two risky assets, Asset A and Asset B. Asset A has an expected return of 12% and a standard deviation of 22%. Asset B has an expected return of 7% and a standard deviation of 11%. The correlation coefficient between the returns of the two assets is 0.32. If an investor allocates 40% of her funds to Asset A and 60% to Asset B, the expected standard deviation of the portfolio is closest to:
questions.hint: Use the formula: sqrt(wA^2 * stdA^2 + wB^2 * stdB^2 + 2*wA*wB*stdA*stdB*corr)
questions.explanation: Calculation is performed using the portfolio variance formula. The portfolio standard deviation is 12.58%.

questions.text: A manufacturing firm operating under US GAAP reports the following financial data for the year ended December 31: Beginning Inventory of $38000, Purchases of $145000, and Ending Inventory of $42000. During the year, the firm recorded an inventory write-down of $8000 due to obsolescence. If the firm had used IFRS instead of US GAAP, and the net realizable value of the inventory subsequently recovered by $12000 in the following year, the most appropriate accounting treatment under IFRS would be to:
options: Reverse the write-down up to the original cost of the inventory, decreasing COGS.
Recognize the recovery as a direct increase to retained earnings.
Ignore the recovery because inventory reversals are prohibited under IFRS.
questions.hint: IFRS allows reversals of inventory write-downs, unlike US GAAP.
questions.explanation: Under IFRS, if the net realizable value of previously written-down inventory recovers, the write-down can be reversed. The reversal is recognized as a reduction in cost of goods sold (COGS) in the period it occurs, capped at the original cost.
